what: EyeDentify, Inc. (Robert 'Buzz' Hill, founded 1976) brought a commercial retinal scanner to market in 1981 after a 1978 patent for the scanning means.
fit: A device that identifies a person by scanning the retinal blood-vessel pattern of the eye and matching it to a stored template.

sources.title: Retinal scan
sources.quote: In 1978, specific means for a retinal scanner was patented, followed by a commercial model in 1981.

note: Same date as second pass. Rejected: Simon/Goldstein 1935 retina idea and Flom/Safir iris concept (no working device); Daugman iris algorithm 1994 (later). A working prototype may predate 1981 (patent 1978) but no dated demonstration was found; no contemporary 1978-1982 source was found on archive.org.
searched: ia_search3 'retinal' 'Eyedentify' 1979-1986 (earliest hits 1984-85); 'retina' 'EyeDentify'/'Eye Dentify' 1980-1984 (0 hits); Wikipedia Retinal scan; leads.

what: EyeDentify 7.5 retinal scanner in use as an access-control device; a 1985 Naval Postgraduate School thesis tested the 7.5 system (dated 1984 model) and Computerworld 1986 reports a Dallas vault firm using it at its guard door.
fit: Machine identifies people at an entrance by scanning retinal vessel patterns, used for real access control.

sources.title: Eye scanner security bows
sources.quote: Eyedentify, Inc. has announced a retinal scanning biometric security device

sources.title: Examination of Retinal Pattern Threshold Levels
sources.quote: The Eye Dentify 7.5 system by Eye Dentify Inc., of Portland, Oregon, proved to be a fairly expensive, highly reliable access contr

note: Earliest dated documentary evidence of fielded/evaluated use is 1984-86 (figure in thesis cites 'Eye Dentify 7.5, 1984'); the actual first customer installation (probably 1981-83) was not found. Date 1984 is a lower-bound estimate; both sources are more than 2 years after 1981 or only document the product, so reference.
searched: As above; leads Computerworld 1986-06-23 and DTIC ADA161213 re-checked FOUND.

concept_note: Kept 1981 demonstration (retina commercial scanner); added a 1984 practical-use lower bound from 1985 thesis; no mass adoption (niche high-security product).

what: Lockheed Missiles & Space Co. (Roger K. Summit) completed the DIALOG online retrieval system, a computer searched from a remote terminal, tested on NASA data at Ames.
fit: A computer stores a large bibliographic file and returns references matching keyword queries interactively in minutes or seconds.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

sources.title: Computer Decisions 1967 (news item on DIALOG)
sources.quote: Since May 1, Ames has been equipped with a DIALOG-fed remote terminal linked by telephone lines to a comput¬ er at LMSC

note: Agrees with second pass. Rejected: Shaw/Bush Rapid Selector 1949 (electro-optical microfilm scanner, 78,000 codes/min, not a computer and not seconds over a large file); MEDLARS (NLM, operating 1964) was batch processing with turnaround of days, not interactive seconds. Contemporary item mentions retrieval 'from hours or days down to minutes or even seconds'.
searched: archive.org full text: MEDLARS searches 1963-65; 'Rapid Selector' microfilm 1947-50; Wikipedia Dialog; lead Computer Decisions item.

what: Ames Research Center began using a DIALOG-fed remote terminal linked by telephone to Lockheed's computer (Summit's project under NASA contract).
fit: Real users (NASA Ames) searched a large technical-literature file by remote terminal and got references in minutes.

sources.title: Computer Decisions 1967 (news item on DIALOG)
sources.quote: Since May 1, Ames has been equipped with a DIALOG-fed remote terminal linked by telephone lines to a comput¬ er at LMSC

note: Year of 'May 1' inferred from the item's 1967-08 record date; Wikipedia/second pass say Ames tests in 1966, so the true date could be a year earlier. Commercial public service followed in 1972.

what: Web search engines such as Google, handling tens of millions of searches a day over a billion indexed pages in under half a second, became everyday tools by about 2000.
fit: Ordinary people routinely query a huge document collection and get matches in a fraction of a second.

sources.title: The W5YI Report
sources.quote: with more than a billion pages indexed which can be accessed in less than half a second

note: Earlier consumer online services (Dialog 1980s, CompuServe) were niche; date is approximate for 'became common'.

concept_note: Kept 1966 Dialog; shifted practical use to the documented Ames terminal (1967 source) and added mass adoption ~2000 (web search); Rapid Selector and MEDLARS rejected.

what: ROBART I, a microprocessor-controlled autonomous sentry robot built by H. R. Everett at the Naval Postgraduate School (1980-82), described in his October 1982 thesis.
fit: A mobile robot that patrols and detects intruders/hazards autonomously as a security sentry.

sources.title: A Microprocessor Controlled Autonomous Sentry Robot
sources.quote: A microprocessor controlled prototype robot was designed and built to perform as an autonomous sentry

sources.title: Security robot report (ROBART)
sources.quote: ROBART I, the original prototype security robot (1981-1982), was built at the Naval Postgraduate School

note: Second pass had only Knightscope 2015 as practical use and no demonstration. Earlier fiction/ideas (1944 claim) not working systems. No earlier working patrol robot found; ROBART is a research prototype, so only demonstration.
searched: archive.org full text 'security robot' patrols 1984-88; 'Denning' robot sentry 1985-88; leads ROBART DTIC items.

what: Denning Mobile Robotics' Sentry, marketed as an autonomous mobile security robot guard patrolling warehouses; prison units ordered by Southern Steel (600 ordered, 8 in advanced testing in late 1985).
fit: A robot that patrols facilities on its own and alerts authorities to intruders, sold to customers for real guard duty.

sources.title: Raising a new generation of robots
sources.quote: mobile se curity robot guard works in: dependently patrolling warehouses and other facilities

sources.title: Denning Sentry robot article
sources.quote: eight of these, destined for prison duty, are now undergoing ad- vanced testing

note: Replaces 2015 Knightscope: Denning Sentry (1985-86) was earlier. The exact first customer patrol deployment date was not found (1985 sources say testing/orders; Dec 1985 Robotics Age lists it as a product). Date 1986 is the earliest source describing it as working patrol service. RoboGuard/Prowler not checked.
searched: As above; Robotics Age 1985-12 product guide; Town Crier 1986-04-30 and 1988-09-14.

concept_note: Moved practical use back from 2015 (Knightscope) to ~1986 (Denning Sentry) and added 1982 ROBART I demonstration. No mass adoption milestone: security robots remain niche; arresting/credential-checking robots not found.

what: Djourno and Eyries in Paris implanted an electrode on the auditory nerve of a deaf patient and stimulated it electrically, producing sound sensations.
fit: An electronic device implanted in the body to restore a sense (hearing) by stimulating the auditory nerve.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: André Djourno and Charles Eyriès invented the original cochlear implant in 1957.

sources.title: Cochlear stimulation article
sources.quote: Depuis les essais thérapeutiques de Ch. EYRIES et A. DJOURNO en 1957, on France, on sait qu'il est possible de rendre une certaine

note: Same as second pass. Earlier candidates: none for neural implants (cardiac pacemakers 1958 are implants but do not restore/extend senses via nerve interface; excluded as outside the neural/sensory framing). The 1974 source is 17 years after the event so is reference.
searched: Wikipedia Cochlear implant; archive.org 'cochlear implant' House 3M 1972-76; leads.

what: Hochmair's multichannel cochlear implant was first implanted in a person in Vienna in December 1977; Clark's followed in 1978 and was commercialized as Nucleus.
fit: Implanted electronic device used in patients to restore hearing for real-world use.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: with the Hochmairs' device first implanted in a person in December 1977 and Clark's in August 1978

note: Kept second pass. The 3M/House single-channel implant (about 1972) was used on patients earlier and could be an earlier practical use, but only a passing mention in a 1972-dated handbook (not fetched) was found, so not adopted. Mass adoption not claimed: about 600,000 recipients worldwide by 2016 is not routine use by ordinary people.

concept_note: Kept cochlear implant 1957 demonstration and 1977-78 practical use; no mass adoption milestone (niche medical device); brain-computer implants and augmentation of memory/ability are later or not realized.

what: SoftBank's Pepper humanoid was introduced in Tokyo on 5 June 2014 and placed in SoftBank Mobile phone stores in Japan to greet and serve customers.
fit: A robot placed in shops to receive and talk with customers as a greeter/receptionist.

sources.title: Pepper (robot)
sources.quote: showcased in SoftBank Mobile phone stores in Japan beginning the next day

note: This is certainly NOT the earliest: web-search snippets (not fetched, not quotable) report robot waiters Tanbo R-1/R-2 at the Two Panda Deli/Restaurant in Pasadena in 1983 (called the first restaurant with robot waiting staff by Guinness) and Ken-chan at Grazie's, Tokyo, 1985; also the RHINO museum tour-guide robot at Deutsches Museum Bonn, May 1997 (first interactive museum tour-guide). Pages for these (cyberneticzoo, paleofuture, gizmodo, Guinness: proxy blocked; Smithsonian: 403; CMU PDFs: unreachable; archive.org books: lending 401/403) could not be fetched, so I could not source them. Pepper kept only as a sourced reference milestone; a later agent should source Tanbo 1983 as the likely true first practical use.
searched: archive.org full text 'robot waiter'/'bartender'/'receptionist' 1970-92 (only fiction), 'Two Panda' robot 1983-90 (only lending books; Science: it's changing your world, 1985, snippet mentions Two Panda Robot Restaurant, Pasadena); WebSearch for first robot waiter/guide; Wikipedia Robotic restaurant, Service robot, Pepper.

concept_note: No first_demonstration given (no fetched source for a working public-serving robot before Pepper). Likely earlier practical use is Tanbo R-1 (Pasadena, 1983) but could not be quoted. No mass adoption: service robots are still niche.
